title: Foundations: who are you, and what may you do?

cards.s: Foundations: who are you, and what may you do?
cards.html: Security on an API boils down to two separate questions, asked in order: who is calling? and are they allowed to do this? Today the AI services answer neither well. The shared X-Password only proves "someone who knows the password", and that someone could be anyone.

• Authentication (often shortened to authn) answers "who are you?". Showing a passport at the airport is authentication.
  • Authorization (authz) answers "what may you do?". The boarding pass that lets you onto one specific flight, not every flight, is authorization.

They fail differently, and HTTP has a separate status code for each:

FailureHTTP codePlain meaningOur example
Authentication failed401 Unauthorized (badly named; it really means "unauthenticated")"I don't know who you are, or your proof is bad"Expired token, forged signature, no header
Authorization failed403 Forbidden"I know exactly who you are, and you may not do this"A valid student token calling a grading endpoint

This split is not academic for us. The apps react differently to each code: on 401 they fetch a new token and retry once, on 403 they give up and report a bug. Getting the code wrong breaks the apps. Section "Roles, scopes, 401 vs 403" goes deeper.

cards.s: A credential is anything that proves identity
cards.html: A password, a fingerprint, an API key and a token are all credentials. The interesting differences are: who has it, how long it lasts, what it says about you, and how the server checks it.

cards.s: Sessions vs tokens: two ways to remember who logged in
cards.html:
HTTP is stateless: each request arrives alone, with no memory of the previous one. So after you log in, the server needs a way to recognise your next request. There are two broad approaches.

Server-side sessions (the cloakroom ticket). You hand in your coat; you get a numbered ticket. The ticket itself means nothing. The cloakroom keeps a list: ticket 47 = the blue coat. Every time you show the ticket, staff look it up.

  • The server stores a session record (in memory, Redis or a database) and gives the client a random session id, usually in a cookie.
  • Every request costs a lookup in that store.
  • Logging someone out is easy: delete the record.
  • Every server that wants to check the session needs access to the same store.

cards.s: Sessions vs tokens: two ways to remember who logged in
cards.html:
Self-contained tokens (the wristband). The token itself carries the facts ("user 141, student, expires 10:15") plus a tamper-proof seal. The server checks the seal and reads the facts. No lookup.

  • Nothing to store on the server. Any service that knows how to check the seal can verify the token, even a service in another language on another host. This is exactly why tokens suit us: Laravel issues, Python verifies, and they never need to talk per request.
  • The trade-off: you can't easily "un-issue" a token. It stays valid until it expires. That's why our tokens live only 15 minutes (5 for the backend). More on this in the revocation part of section "Security pitfalls".

cards.s: Sessions vs tokens: two ways to remember who logged in
cards.html:
A cookie is a small named value (for example session=8f3a…) that a website asks your browser to keep. The server sends it once in a response header:

Set-Cookie: session=8f3a…; HttpOnly; Secure; Max-Age=7776000

From then on the browser attaches it automatically to every request to that same site:

Cookie: session=8f3a…

cards.s: Sessions vs tokens: two ways to remember who logged in
cards.html:
So the cookie is the pocket where the cloakroom ticket lives. You don't have to show it by hand; the browser does it for you on every visit, until it expires or you log out. Three flags matter for login cookies:

  • HttpOnly: JavaScript on the page can't read it, so a malicious script can't steal it.
  • Secure: it is only sent over HTTPS, never over plain HTTP.
  • SameSite: it isn't sent when another website triggers the request, which blocks most cross-site tricks.

This app works exactly like that: when you log in, the server sets an HttpOnly cookie with a random session id and keeps only a hash of it. That's why you stay logged in after closing the app.

cards.s: Sessions vs tokens: two ways to remember who logged in
cards.html:
Tokens can travel in a cookie too, but our ai_token travels in a header instead (see "Bearer tokens" below), because the AI API is called from apps, not just browsers.

Laravel's normal login token (from Passport, the Laravel OAuth library) stays as it is and is sent only to Laravel APIs. The new ai_token is a separate self-contained token, sent only to the AI API. Two tokens, two audiences.

A bearer token is a token where "whoever bears (holds) it may use it", like cash or a concert ticket. There is no extra proof that the holder is the rightful owner. It travels in a standard header:

Authorization: Bearer eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjIwMjYtMTEifQ.eyJ...

Because anyone who steals it can use it, a bearer token must only travel over HTTPS, must never be logged, and should be short-lived. Those three rules come back again and again.

cards.s: What we have today, and why it's weak
cards.html:
Today every caller sends the same header:

X-Password: <shared password>

cards.s: What we have today, and why it's weak
cards.html:
The AI guide sums up the problems in a table; here they are with the reasoning behind each:

PropertyX-Password todayWhy it matters
Who knows itEvery caller: every app build, the Laravel backend, every developerA secret shared by many is not a secret. The React guide states it plainly: anything in the React build, including REACT_APP_* and VITE_* values, ends up in the public JS bundle, "that's how the old password leaked". Mobile apps can be unpacked the same way.
LifetimeNever expiresOne leak works forever, until someone changes it everywhere at once.
IdentityNone: "no idea who is calling"You can't log per user, rate-limit per university or tell a student from the grading cron.
PermissionsAll or nothingWhoever has the password can call grading, chatbot, exam risk, everything.
RotationChanging it breaks every app until each is rebuilt and shippedSo in practice it never changes.

cards.s: What we have today, and why it's weak
cards.html: This is what the pentest flagged (EX-3055). The guide adds a sobering line for the end of the migration: the old password "is in git history and old app builds, so treat it as public".

The current scheme was described as "secret password / IP based": besides the password, some AI hosts only accept traffic from known IP addresses. An IP allowlist is a list of source addresses a server (or its firewall) accepts.

It helps for server-to-server calls, such as Laravel backend to grading, because those come from a few fixed addresses. It can't protect the endpoints that apps call directly from students' phones and browsers, because those come from any address on the internet. #### Can't an attacker just fake their IP address?

Mostly not, for web traffic. HTTP runs over TCP, and a TCP connection starts with a three-way handshake: the client says hello, the server answers to the source address, and the client must reply to that answer. If an attacker writes a fake source address on their packets, the server's answer goes to the fake address, not to the attacker. The attacker never sees it, the handshake never completes, and no HTTP request is ever delivered. Faking an IP only works for one-way traffic (which is why it shows up in flooding attacks), not for a real conversation like an API call.

The allowlist is still weaker than it looks, for other reasons:

  • Trusting a header instead of the connection. Behind a proxy, apps often read the client IP from X-Forwarded-For. That is just text the caller writes. If the app trusts it from anyone, an attacker sends X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.5 and walks in. Only trust it when it was set by your own proxy.
  • Borrowing an allowed address. An attacker who breaks into any machine on the allowed network, or shares the same cloud or office exit address, sends traffic from an allowed IP for real.
  • It says where, not who. An allowed address can carry many programs and people; the server still can't tell them apart.

So an IP allowlist is a useful extra lock for a few fixed servers, never a replacement for a credential. The JWT guides don't mention IP allowlisting at all, so what to do with it is an open decision for the AI team. The "Rollout" section gives a recommendation.

quiz.q: A valid token is sent but lacks the needed permission. Which status?
quiz.why: 401 = not authenticated (no/bad token); 403 = authenticated but not allowed.

o: only the bearer's IP may use it
whoever holds it can use it, so it must be kept secret
They contain everything needed to verify them, with no server-side session lookup
quiz.why: The signature and claims are self-contained.

quiz.q: A shared X-Password header proves which user is calling.
quiz.why: Myth. Everyone shares it; it identifies no user, can't carry permissions and leaks easily.
